components.label: Tenant application
components.responsibility: Own application queries and transaction intent.

components.label: Authenticated query gateway
components.responsibility: Derive tenant identity from credentials; reject caller-controlled cross-tenant routing.

components.label: Database data plane
components.responsibility: Own transactions, indexes, WAL and database-enforced roles.

components.label: Provisioning API
components.responsibility: Validate tenant requests and commit desired state before reporting accepted.

components.label: Desired-state registry
components.responsibility: Persist desired versions, operation deduplication and observations.

components.label: Provisioning reconciler
components.responsibility: Retry provider operations using stable resource identities and generation checks.

components.label: Tenant route directory
components.responsibility: Publish epoch-versioned tenant-to-database roles and endpoints.

components.label: Shared connection broker
components.responsibility: Set and reset tenant context for every checkout; never trust connection leftovers.

components.label: Tenant admission policy
components.responsibility: Enforce per-tenant and global outstanding-work limits.

components.label: Backup coordinator
components.responsibility: Create engine-consistent backups and retain encryption-key references without exposing secrets.

components.label: Restore verifier
components.responsibility: Restore to an isolated target and validate data before it becomes routable.

components.label: Cutover coordinator
components.responsibility: Fence writes, advance routing epoch and reconcile uncertain operations at migration.

components.label: Unified lifecycle controller
components.responsibility: Own reconcile and cutover transitions under one durable desired generation.

requirements.text: Authenticate every request and enforce tenant isolation through routing and database authorization.
Reconcile durable desired state with idempotent provisioning and explicit observed status.
Apply tenant quotas and bounded admission without claiming simulation concurrency maps directly to CPU.
Back up and restore consistently; fence migrations and verify the restored data before cutover.

problem.scope: Study a control plane that provisions database access and a separate data plane. This design delegates transactions, WAL and replication to a real database engine rather than inventing a database in an API wrapper.

provenance.note: Authored interview preparation. Technical references support mechanisms, not the claim that a company asked this question.

acceptanceCases.given: Tenant A and B share a gateway or pool.
acceptanceCases.then: Authentication-derived scoping and database permissions prevent access to B.
acceptanceCases.when: A forges tenant B in a query and a pooled session is reused.

acceptanceCases.given: Provider created a resource but the controller lost its reply.
acceptanceCases.then: Discover and adopt the stable resource ID; no second resource is created.
acceptanceCases.when: Restart reconciliation with the same desired generation.

acceptanceCases.given: Tenant A fills its concurrency budget.
acceptanceCases.then: A gets bounded overload; B retains its configured share, subject to global capacity.
acceptanceCases.when: A and B submit another query.

acceptanceCases.given: A verified checkpoint and WAL are retained.
acceptanceCases.then: Validate schema, checksums and committed records through the stated position.
acceptanceCases.when: Restore to a fresh isolated target.

acceptanceCases.given: Old and new targets coexist during migration.
acceptanceCases.then: Old target rejects the stale write and the client receives an explicit retry/uncertain outcome.
acceptanceCases.when: A delayed write uses the old route epoch after cutover.

guarantees: A retry cannot create an unrelated duplicate database or publish stale status.

assumptions: The database engine supplies durable transactional behavior.
Capacity promises require measured resource qualification, not simulation parameter conversion.
solutions.chooseWhen: Strong fault and performance isolation justifies per-tenant resource overhead.

invariants: Tenant identity is authenticated, not accepted from an arbitrary URL.
stages.question: What can the tenant request?
stages.reason: Begin with an application and a logical database boundary.
stages.title: Separate tenant intent from service

invariants: Gateway retries do not invent transaction success.
stages.question: Who owns transaction state?
stages.reason: Expand the service into query validation and the actual storage engine.
stages.title: Expose the data-plane boundary

invariants: Accepted means desired state is durable, not that a database is ready.
stages.question: Does an accepted request survive a controller crash?
stages.reason: Introduce a separate control API and durable desired-state registry.
stages.title: Persist provisioning intent

invariants: Stale desired generations cannot publish ready for a newer request.
stages.question: What happens after a partial provider success?
stages.reason: Add a controller whose retries use stable resource IDs and generation guards.
stages.title: Reconcile resources to desired state

invariants: Never reuse a pooled session with another tenant context still installed.
stages.question: How do queries reach the correct isolation boundary?
stages.reason: Make tenant routing and pooled-session reset obligations explicit.
stages.title: Route tenants to dedicated endpoints

invariants: All terminal query paths release admission permits.
stages.question: How is one tenant prevented from exhausting the pool?
stages.reason: Add tenant and global admission before database work.
stages.title: Bound per-tenant work

invariants: A backup manifest without a successful restore is not recovery proof.
stages.question: Is a backup usable or merely present?
stages.reason: Add engine-consistent backup and isolated restore verification.
stages.title: Prove restore before routing it

invariants: Only the new epoch becomes writable after cutover; old targets reject stale epochs.

operations.reason: One durable lifecycle state machine owns provisioning and cutover epochs.

stages.question: Can an old route still accept writes during migration?
stages.reason: Add write fencing and join lifecycle decisions under one desired generation.
stages.title: Unify reconciliation and fenced cutover

solutions.title: Dedicated tenant data planes
tradeoffs: Idle resources and fleet upgrades cost more.
Tenant placement and provisioning still need a control plane.
